forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley lifts capital spending to £31m as debt falls and treasury returns beat forecast
news_drafts.lead: Burnley Council revised its capital spending upward by £6.2m to £31m in the first quarter of 2026–27, an 82 per cent increase on the previous year, but financed most of the rise through grants and reserves rather than new borrowing. The council's underlying borrowing need, known as its capital financing requirement, fell by £2.3m to £88.1m despite the higher spending, and its external debt decreased by £234k as scheduled repayments came due. Investment returns and debt management outperformed budget by £120k in the quarter. The council forecasts capital spending will fall sharply to £13.6m next year, suggesting the present level is a peak in a frontloaded programme. Financing costs are forecast to reach 24–28 per cent of the council's net revenue stream, nearly double the 14.7 per cent recorded in 2025–26, reflecting both elevated capital investment and the impact of higher interest rates on debt service.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley received "Reasonable Assurance" audit opinion for 2025/26 but Charter Walk acquisition had comprehensive controls
news_drafts.lead: Burnley's internal audit concluded that the council has a good system of controls but minor weaknesses in design or consistency of application may put the achievement of some objectives at risk. The council received a "Reasonable Assurance" overall audit opinion for 2025/26, the second-highest rating available. However, when auditors reviewed the council's acquisition of Charter Walk shopping centre in Burnley town centre — a decision presenting wide-ranging commercial risks — they found the risks were properly identified, controlled and continue to be monitored, and members were fully briefed before the decision. Internal audit gave comprehensive assurance that controls were sound and consistently applied, with no remedial actions required. The council implemented 100 per cent of high-priority audit recommendations against its 100 per cent target, though some lower-priority recommendations have been delayed.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley plans £31.0m capital budget while keeping borrowing limits, with £120k forecast saving
news_drafts.lead:
Burnley Borough Council is paying for its building and equipment schemes largely from its own cash rather than taking new loans, and expects that to save £120,000 this year, according to papers for Full Council on 23 September 2026. Its first-quarter treasury report (treasury management is how a council borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both) shows total borrowing of £62.670m.

The council's capital budget, money spent on things that last, such as buildings, roads and equipment, has risen from £24.832m to £31.025m, an increase of £6.2m. Its borrowing need has risen from £8.442m to £9.261m, up £0.8m. The council describes itself as "under-borrowed": it has borrowed less than it needs, using its own cash (internal borrowing) instead of taking loans. It says it is deferring external borrowing because bank rates are high.

Because the council remains under-borrowed, the report says its existing limits on borrowing, the Operational Boundary and the Authorised Limit (the maximum total debt it has told itself it will not exceed), are "still deemed prudent". No policy changes are proposed.

The council's revenue monitoring report, which checks day-to-day spending against budget, says the treasury position reflects a net saving "as has been the case in recent years". It adds that "the sustainability of this position remains under continual review".

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Q1 Appendix 1 - Pru Ind working papers Q1 Final
findings.headline: Financing costs forecast to reach 24–28% of net revenue stream, nearly double the 2025/26 level of 14.7%.
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast in the 24–28% range for the coming period, nearly double the 14.7% recorded in 2025/26. This sharp increase reflects both the elevated capital investment and the impact of higher interest rates on debt service. The council notes that net revenue stream assumptions for future years are based on 2026/27 levels and will be revised as part of MTFS updates, suggesting the ratio may move as the revenue base is reassessed.
findings.matters: Financing costs as a percentage of revenue is a core affordability indicator. A near-doubling in a single year indicates debt service is becoming a significantly larger claim on the council's revenue budget, potentially constraining flexibility for service delivery and signalling the need for careful debt management going forward.
findings.figures: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream: 14.7% (2025/26 actual) to 24.4%–28.6% (2026/27 forecast period), moderating to 24.1%–25.0% in later years
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream* 14.7% 28.6% 24.4% 24.2% 25.0% 24.1%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Q1 Appendix 1 - Pru Ind working papers Q1 Final
findings.headline: Capital expenditure spiked to £31 million for current year 2026/27 (revised estimate), 82% above prior year and well above the original forecast.
findings.detail: Burnley's capital expenditure for 2026/27 has been revised upward to £31,025k, compared to £17,047k actually spent in 2025/26 and the £24,332k originally estimated for the current year. The revision represents an 82% increase from the prior year and a 27% upward revision from the original plan. Capital expenditure is then forecast to decline sharply to £13,605k in 2027/28 and continue declining thereafter, suggesting this is a one-year peak in a planned, but frontloaded, capital programme.
findings.matters: A significant one-year spike in capital expenditure signals either new projects approved, existing schemes accelerated, or cost escalation brought forward into the current year. Lenders assessing borrowing requirements need to understand what is driving this concentration and when expenditure normalises; peer councils monitor whether this reflects genuine demand or budget management.
findings.figures: Capital Expenditure: £17,047k (2025/26 actual), £31,025k (2026/27 revised estimate), £13,605k (2027/28), declining to £10,077k by 2029/30

findings.headline: Council forecasts net treasury management saving of £120k for 2026-27, indicating positive investment and debt management performance
findings.detail: Against a full-year budget of £475k for interest and dividend income, Q1 returns were £66k. The council is now forecasting a net treasury saving of £120k for the year, suggesting investment returns and borrowing cost management are outperforming budget expectations.
findings.matters: A positive treasury variance demonstrates effective debt portfolio and investment management. In a period of economic weakness and inflationary pressure, a forecast saving shows the council is capturing value from short-term investments (achieving 3.60% average return) and managing borrowing costs efficiently.
findings.figures: Interest receivable Q1: £66k; full-year budget for interest and dividends: £475k; forecast net saving: £120k. Average investment return: 3.60%
findings.quote: The current forecast for the year is a net Treasury Management saving of (£120k).

findings.headline: Council took no new borrowing in Q1 despite £6.2m capital budget increase and repaid £234k of existing debt
findings.detail: The council did not enter any temporary market loans for cash flow purposes during April–June. External debt fell by £234k from £62.9m to £62.7m through a scheduled annuity repayment on PWLB loans. This means the entire £6.2m capital budget revision was financed from grants, revenue, and existing cash reserves without new borrowing.
findings.matters: Taking no new debt despite a major upward revision in capital spending demonstrates strong cash management and independent financing. It reduces reliance on debt markets at a time of elevated gilt yields (10-year yields reached 5.18% in May) and shows the council can fund growth from its own resources or grant funding.
findings.figures: External debt 1 April 2026: £62,904k; 30 June 2026: £62,670k; Change: –£234k. PWLB debt: £62,890k to £62,656k
findings.quote: PWLB Loans – No maturity loan repayments were made during the period 1 April to 30 June 2026. One scheduled annuity repayment was made during the period totaling £234k.

findings.headline: Capital financing requirement revised down £2.3m to £88.1m despite higher capital spending, showing improved cash position
findings.detail: The CFR (underlying borrowing need for capital) was estimated at £90.4m in the Treasury Management Strategy approved in March but revised down to £88.1m at Q1. This reduction of 2.5% occurs despite the capital budget rising by £6.2m, indicating the council's actual cash requirements are lower than the March forecast or that financing is more efficient.
findings.matters: A downward revision in CFR shows the council has better cash access or is using alternative financing more efficiently than planned. This reduces long-term debt need and borrowing costs, improving financial flexibility and debt serviceability—key metrics lenders monitor.
findings.figures: CFR estimate March 2026: £90.391m; CFR estimate Q1 2026: £88.114m; reduction: £2.277m
findings.quote: The Council's capital financing requirement (CFR) for 2026/27 was estimated at £90.391m and approved as part of the TMSS in March 2026. At Q1, based on approved capital slippage from 2025/26, the Council's draft Statement of Accounts for 25/26 and in year capital budget adjustments, this is now estimated at £88.114m.
